1.note: See how you translated the similar expression in [7:1](ta:07).

1.q: ב⁠שנת הָ⁠עֲשִׂרִ֔ית לְ⁠צִדְקִיָּ֖הוּ מֶ֣לֶךְ יְהוּדָ֑ה הִ֧יא הַ⁠שָּׁנָ֛ה שְׁמֹנֶֽה־עֶשְׂרֵ֥ה שָׁנָ֖ה לִ⁠נְבֽוּכַדְרֶאצַּֽר
1.note: If your language would not represent a number in a form such as **the tenth year** and **the eighteenth year**, you could represent this number in a form that your language would use. Alternate translation: [in year ten of Zedekiah the king of Judah—that was year eighteen of Nebuchadnezzar]

2.note: The words that the ULT translates as **And … and** indicate that the army of the king of Babylon **was laying siege** to Jerusalem at the same time as when Jeremiah **was shut up** in the courtyard of the guard, which was the same time that a word from Yahweh “was to Jeremiah,” mentioned in the previous verse. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could describe the time relationship more explicitly. Alternate translation: [While the army of the king of Babylon was laying siege to Jerusalem, Jeremiah the prophet was shut up in the courtyard of the guard]

2.q: וְ⁠יִרְמְיָ֣הוּ הַ⁠נָּבִ֗יא הָיָ֤ה כָלוּא֙ בַּ⁠חֲצַ֣ר הַ⁠מַּטָּרָ֔ה
2.note: The expression **was shut up** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is Zedekiah the king of Judah. Alternate translation: [and Zedekiah the king of Judah held Jeremiah the prophet captive in the courtyard of the guard]

A **courtyard of the guard** is a kind of enclosed area attached to a palace where prisoners were kept under guard. If your readers would not be familiar with what a courtyard of the guard is, you could use a more general term or explain it in a footnote. Alternate translation: [in an enclosed courtyard where prisoners were kept under guard]

3.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 2:5. This also occurs in verses 14, 15, 28, 36, and 42 of this chapter.

3.q: כְּלָא֔⁠וֹ צִדְקִיָּ֥הוּ מֶֽלֶךְ־יְהוּדָ֖ה לֵ⁠אמֹ֑ר מַדּוּעַ֩ אַתָּ֨ה נִבָּ֜א
3.note: Zedekiah is using the question form to begin a lengthy rebuke of Jeremiah for prophesying that Yahweh would give Jerusalem into the hand of the king of Babylon. This question continues to the end of verse 5. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [**the king of Judah had shut him up, saying, ‘You should not be prophesying**]
See how you translated the similar expression in 31:8. This also occurs in verses 7, 17, 24, 27, 28, and 37 of this chapter. Alternate translation: [I am about to give this city]

Here, **hand** represents the power or control of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [into the control of the king of Babylon]

4.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 22:25. This also occurs in verses 24, 25, 28, and 43.

The expression **for being given** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is Yahweh. Alternate translation: [for Yahweh will certainly hand him over]

Jeremiah is repeating forms of the verb **given** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [he will certainly be given into the hand of the king of Babylon]

Jeremiah is using **his mouth will speak with his mouth, and his eyes will see his eyes** as a common expression of the culture to mean that Zedekiah and the king of Babylon will meet together in person, face to face. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he will speak to the king of Babylon in person and see him face to face] or [he will meet the king of Babylon in person]

5.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 1:8. This also occurs in verses 30 and 44.
See how you translated this name in 21:4.
See how you translated the similar expression in 21:14.

6.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 1:4. This also occurs in verses 8 and 26.
The term **saying** introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent this term explicitly.

7.note: See how you translated this name in 22:11.
See how you translated this name in [1:1](ta:01). This also occurs in verses 8 and 9.

The phrase “**the right of redemption**” refers to the legal obligation of the closest male relative to buy back property that a family member was forced to sell; this is done in order to keep it in the family. If your readers would not be familiar with this custom, you could use a more general term or explain it in a footnote. Alternate translation: [you are the closest relative, and so it is your duty to buy it]

7.q: קְנֵ֣ה לְ⁠ךָ֗ אֶת־שָׂדִ⁠י֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר בַּ⁠עֲנָת֔וֹת כִּ֥י לְ⁠ךָ֛ מִשְׁפַּ֥ט הַ⁠גְּאֻלָּ֖ה לִ⁠קְנֽוֹת
7.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about who has the right of redemption before the information about buying the field. Alternate translation: [“Buy for yourself my field that is in Anathoth, since **you have** the right of redemption, and so may buy {it}.”]

8.note: This was an open area attached to the king’s palace that was surrounded by buildings and in which they kept prisoners. See how you translated this in Jeremiah 32:2.

Jeremiah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and to you belongs the right of redemption]

9.note: A shekel is 11 grams. Alternate translation: [17 shekels] or [187 grams]

10.q: וָ⁠אֶכְתֹּ֤ב בַּ⁠סֵּ֨פֶר֙ וָֽ⁠אֶחְתֹּ֔ם וָ⁠אָעֵ֖ד עֵדִ֑ים וָ⁠אֶשְׁקֹ֥ל הַ⁠כֶּ֖סֶף בְּ⁠מֹאזְנָֽיִם
10.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about the witnesses testifying with the information about writing and sealing the document, rather than treating it as a separate step. Alternate translation: [I wrote in the document and sealed it while witnesses watched, and then I weighed the silver on the scales]

The implication is that Jeremiah had witnesses present who watched him buy the field and sign the deed, so that the transaction would be officially confirmed. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and I had witnesses watch me do it]

11.note: The expression **being sealed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [that someone had sealed]

A **seal** is a mark made by pressing a stamp into wax or clay to close a document and show that it has not been opened or changed. If your readers would not be familiar with what a seal is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [the one that was closed with an official mark]

The implication is that the sealed document stated the exact terms and conditions of the purchase agreement. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the commandment and the terms of the purchase agreement]

The expression **and the one being open** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and the copy that no one had sealed]

12.note: The open area attached to the king’s palace that was surrounded by buildings and in which they kept prisoners. See how you translated this in Jeremiah 32:2.

13.note: The pronoun **their** refers to Hanamel, the witnesses, and all the Judeans who were sitting in the courtyard, mentioned in the previous verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [before the eyes of Hanamel, the witnesses, and all the Judeans]

14.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 7:3.
See how you translated this name in 20:12. This also occurs in verse 18.
See how you translated the similar expression in 29:4.

15.q: כִּ֣י כֹ֥ה אָמַ֛ר יְהוָ֥ה צְבָא֖וֹת אֱלֹהֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל
15.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 29:4.

16.note: The phrase **the document of the purchase** refers to a legal document that recorded the sale of the field, as the following verses make clear. Jeremiah assumes that readers will understand this. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the legal document recording the purchase]

17.note: Jeremiah is using the term **Behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Indeed]

Jeremiah is stating the pronoun **you** separately, even though the verb translated as **you made** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that Yahweh himself is the one who made the heavens and the earth. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [you, indeed you alone, made the heavens]
See how you translated the similar expression in 23:24.
See how you translated the similar expression in 27:5.

The abstract noun **power** refers to the ability that Yahweh has to do things. If your language does not use an abstract noun for this idea, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [because you are so powerful]

Jeremiah is using **your outstretched arm** as a common expression of the culture to mean strength or power in action. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and by your mighty power in action] or [and by the powerful things you did]

18.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 14:20.
See how you translated the similar expression in 31:35.

19.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 16:17.
See how you translated the similar expression in 17:10.
See how you translated the similar expression in 17:10.

20.note: Here the author (Jeremiah, quoting his own prayer) is providing background information to help readers understand what happens next in the story. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.
Yahweh is using the term **name** to represent his reputation. Alternate translation: [and you made yourself famous]

21.note: Here, **and with a strong hand and with an outstretched arm** represents power. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and by your mighty strength]

21.q: וַ⁠תֹּצֵ֛א אֶת־עַמְּ⁠ךָ֥ אֶת־יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל מֵ⁠אֶ֣רֶץ מִצְרָ֑יִם בְּ⁠אֹת֣וֹת וּ⁠בְ⁠מוֹפְתִ֗ים
21.note: The implication is that Yahweh performed miracles when he brought his people Israel out of Egypt, from slavery to freedom. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [And by performing miracles, you brought out your people Israel from the land of Egypt]

The implication is that Yahweh caused the Egyptians to be greatly terrified by the plagues and by what happened to their army at the Sea of Reeds. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and by causing the Egyptians to be greatly terrified]

22.note: Jeremiah is using the term **fathers** to mean “ancestors.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you swore to their ancestors to give to them]
See how you translated the similar expression in 11:5.

23.note: The pronoun **it** refers to the land. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the promised land]
See how you translated the similar expression in 26:5.
See how you translated the similar expression in 3:13.

Jeremiah is using **and in your law they did not walk** as a common expression of the culture to mean “they did not obey your law.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and they did not live by your law] or [and they did not obey your law]

If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about the law before the information about their voice. Alternate translation: [and they did not walk in your law, but they did not listen to your voice]

24.note: Jeremiah is using the term **Behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Look]

Jeremiah is speaking of **the siege mounds have come to the city** as if they were a living thing that could travel. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the enemy soldiers have built siege mounds up against the city]

Here, **to** marks “capture it” as the goal or purpose of the siege mounds being brought against the city. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [in order to capture it]

The expression **the city has been given** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is Yahweh. Alternate translation: [Yahweh has given the city]

Here, **hand** represents the power/control of the Chaldeans. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [into the control of the Chaldeans]

24.q: וְ⁠הָ⁠עִ֣יר נִתְּנָ֗ה בְּ⁠יַ֤ד הַ⁠כַּשְׂדִּים֙ הַ⁠נִּלְחָמִ֣ים עָלֶ֔י⁠הָ מִ⁠פְּנֵ֛י הַ⁠חֶ֥רֶב וְ⁠הָ⁠רָעָ֖ב וְ⁠הַ⁠דָּ֑בֶר
24.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Because of the sword and the famine and the plague, the city has been given into the hand of the Chaldeans who are fighting against it]
See how you translated the similar expression in 14:12. This also occurs in verse 36.

Jeremiah is using **because of the face of** as a common expression of the culture to mean “because of” or “on account of.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [due to the warfare] or [because of the battles]

25.note: Jeremiah uses the word **Yet** here to indicate a contrast between the city being given over into the hand of the Chaldeans and Yahweh’s command for Jeremiah to buy the field. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [But despite this,]

Jeremiah is stating the pronoun **you** separately, even though the verb translated as **you said** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that Yahweh did something very unexpected. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [Yet it was you who said]

Jeremiah uses the word **though** here to indicate a contrast between his instruction to buy the field, which was a sign of hope for the future, and the city having fallen to their enemies, which suggested there was no hope. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [even now that the city has been given into the hand of the Chaldeans]

The expression **has been given** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is Yahweh. Alternate translation: [though Yahweh has given the city into the hand of the Chaldeans]
See how you translated the similar expression in 21:4.

26.note: See how you translated the similar expression in [7:1](ta:07).
See how you translated the similar expression in 28:12.

27.note: Yahweh is using the term **Behold** to focus Jeremiah’s attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Listen]

Yahweh is using the possessive form **the God of all flesh** to describe himself as the God who rules over every living creature. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the God who rules over all living creatures]
See how you translated the similar expression in 12:12.

Yahweh is using the question form to emphasize that nothing is too difficult for him. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Nothing is too difficult for me!]

28.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 18:13.

Yahweh is using **Behold me** as an expression that people of this culture would commonly use to mean that he was about to do something. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Now I am about to give this city]
See how you translated the similar expression in 21:4.
See how you translated the similar expression in 21:7.

29.note: These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [will come and set this city on fire and burn it down completely]

Here, **so as to** marks **provoke me** as the goal or purpose of **made smoke to Baal and poured out drink offerings to other gods**. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose.

30.note: The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [This is because]

Jeremiah is speaking as if the people of Israel and the people of Judah were actually the **sons** of those nations’ ancestors. Alternate translation: [the descendants of Israel and the descendants of Judah]
See how you translated the similar expression in 3:5.
See how you translated the similar expression in 1:16.

31.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 21:5. This also occurs in verse 37.

The term translated as **so that** indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes this clear. Alternate translation: [This is why I will remove it]

Yahweh is using **from by my face** as a common expression of the culture to mean “from my presence.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [out of my sight] or [away from me]

32.q: כָּל־רָעַ֨ת בְּנֵֽי־יִשְׂרָאֵ֜ל וּ⁠בְנֵ֣י יְהוּדָ֗ה אֲשֶׁ֤ר עָשׂוּ֙
32.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **evil**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [all the evil things that the sons of Israel and the sons of Judah did]
See how you translated the similar expression in 32:30.
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **anger**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to make me angry]

33.note: Yahweh is using **turned to me the neck and not the face** as a common expression of the culture to mean “turned away from me instead of paying attention to me.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [turned their backs to me instead of facing me] or [rejected me instead of paying attention to me]

Yahweh is using **rising early and teaching** as a common expression of the culture to mean doing something with persistent, repeated effort. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [teaching them again and again] or [teaching them persistently]

Yahweh uses the word **but** here to indicate a contrast between his teaching them and their not listening. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [yet they were not listening to receive instruction]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **instruction**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to receive what I taught them]

34.q: וַ⁠יָּשִׂ֣ימוּ שִׁקּֽוּצֵי⁠הֶ֗ם בַּ⁠בַּ֛יִת אֲשֶׁר־נִקְרָֽא־שְׁמִ֥⁠י עָלָ֖י⁠ו לְ⁠טַמְּאֽ⁠וֹ
34.note: Setting up idols in Yahweh’s temple was a symbolic action by which the people of Israel and Judah showed that they rejected Yahweh as their God and worshiped other gods instead. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [And they set up idols to worship other gods in the house which is belongs to me, and so they defiled it]
See how you translated this same phrase in 7:10.

Here, **to defile it** marks defiling the temple as the goal or purpose of setting their detestable things in the house which is called by Yahweh’s name. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose.

35.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 19:5.
See how you translated the similar expression in 19:2.

The act of **making their sons and their daughters pass through to Molech** was a symbolic action by which the Israelites offered their children as human sacrifices to the god Molech. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [making their sons and their daughters pass through fire as offerings to Molech]
See how you translated the similar expression in 3:16.

The abstract noun **abomination** refers to something detestable. If your language does not use an abstract noun for this idea, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to do this detestable thing]

By **so as to cause Judah to sin**, Yahweh means that by building these high places and sacrificing their children to Molech, the people led the rest of Judah into sinning against him by worshiping false gods. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [so as to cause Judah to be liable for punishment]

36.note: The term translated as **therefore** indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes this clear. Alternate translation: [This is why]
See how you translated the similar expression in 21:4.

37.note: Yahweh is using **Behold me** as an expression that people of this culture would commonly use to mean that they were about to do something. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Now I am about to gather them]

It might seem that the expression **where I drove them there** contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [to which I drove them]
See how you translated the similar expression in 23:8.
See how you translated the similar expression in 21:5.

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **anger**, **heat**, and **fury**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [because I was very angry with them]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **security**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and cause them to dwell securely]

38.q: וְ⁠הָ֥יוּ לִ֖⁠י לְ⁠עָ֑ם וַ⁠אֲנִ֕י אֶהְיֶ֥ה לָ⁠הֶ֖ם לֵ⁠אלֹהִֽים
38.note: The pronoun **I myself** refers to Yahweh, while the pronoun **their** refers to the people of Israel and Judah. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And they will be my people, and I, Yahweh, will be their God]

Yahweh is using the possessive form **their God** to describe himself as the one whom his people worship. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and I myself will be the God whom they worship]

39.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 5:4.
Here, **to fear me** marks fearing Yahweh as the goal or purpose of Yahweh giving them one heart and one way. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose.

Jeremiah is using **all the days** as a common expression of the culture to mean “continually” or “always.” See how you translated the this expression in 31:36. Alternate translation: [every day] or [continually]
Yahweh is speaking as if the people of Israel were actually the **sons** of the people he is addressing. Alternate translation: [and to their descendants after them]

40.note: Cutting an animal in pieces was a symbolic action by which people in ancient times formalized a covenant. Here, Yahweh speaks of establishing an everlasting covenant with his people using this same expression, **cut … a covenant**, to show that he is solemnly binding himself to do good to them forever. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [And I will solemnly establish for them an everlasting covenant]

This is a double negative, consisting of the negative particle **not** and the negative word **turn back**. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use a positive expression to translate this. Alternate translation: [I will always remain faithful]

Here, **to do good to them** marks doing good to them as the goal or purpose of the everlasting covenant that Yahweh will make with his people. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose.

40.q: וְ⁠אֶת־יִרְאָתִ⁠י֙ אֶתֵּ֣ן בִּ⁠לְבָבָ֔⁠ם לְ⁠בִלְתִּ֖י ס֥וּר מֵ⁠עָלָֽ⁠י
40.note: Here, **so that** marks **they will not turn aside from by me** as the goal or purpose of **I will put my fear in their heart**. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose.

41.note: Here, **to do good to them** marks the goal or purpose of Yahweh rejoicing over his people. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [to benefit them]

Yahweh is speaking of the people of Israel as if they were a plant that he could **plant** in the ground. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and I will settle them permanently in this land]
The abstract noun **faithfulness** can be expressed with an adjective such as “faithful.” Alternate translation: [and I will faithfully plant them in this land]
See how you translated the similar expression in 3:10.

Here Yahweh is speaking of himself as if he had a **being**, like a human does, in order to express that he will act with the entirety of who he is. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and with everything that I am] or [and completely]

42.q: כַּ⁠אֲשֶׁ֤ר הֵבֵ֨אתִי֙ אֶל־הָ⁠עָ֣ם הַ⁠זֶּ֔ה אֵ֛ת כָּל־הָ⁠רָעָ֥ה הַ⁠גְּדוֹלָ֖ה הַ⁠זֹּ֑את כֵּ֣ן אָנֹכִ֞י מֵבִ֤יא עֲלֵי⁠הֶם֙ אֶת־כָּל־הַ⁠טּוֹבָ֔ה אֲשֶׁ֥ר אָנֹכִ֖י & דֹּבֵ֥ר עֲלֵי⁠הֶֽם
42.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **I brought to this people all this great calamity** is characteristic of Yahweh punishing his people, so is **I am bringing upon them all the good that I am speaking concerning them** characteristic of Yahweh blessing them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [In the same way that I brought all this great disaster on this people, so I will bring them all the good things that I am promising them]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **calamity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [all these disastrous things]

43.note: The word **field** is singular in form, but it refers to fields in general, not to one specific field. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Fields will be bought]

The expression **will be bought** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is the people of Israel. Alternate translation: [People will buy fields]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **desolation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [is a deserted place]
See how you translated the similar expression in 4:25.

The people are not referring to a specific **beast**. They mean **beasts** in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and animals]

The expression **it has been given** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is the Chaldeans. Alternate translation: [the Chaldeans have taken it]

Here, **hand** represents the power/control/capability of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [into the power of the Chaldeans]

44.note: Jeremiah is repeating forms of the verb **witness** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [and having witnesses formally witness the transaction]
